hook.line: Stone boards with rows of pits, thought to date back at least to the 6th–7th century, have been found at sites in Ethiopia and Eritrea.
hook.say: Let’s set off on a sowing-game journey!

ch.say: It spread from Africa to the world.
p: Mancala is the family name for “sowing” games played across Africa and beyond. The word is said to come from Arabic for “to move”.
With trade and migration it reached the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas.

ch.say: Easy to play anywhere — so it’s everywhere.
tl: Pitted boards at sites of the Aksumite kingdom
Spreads along Arab and East African trade routes
Said to cross the Atlantic to the Caribbean
Oware is solved by computer: a draw

ch.say: Scoop up the seeds and drop them one at a time.
ch.cap: Two rows of six pits plus a store at each end (Kalah style)
p: Scoop all the seeds from one of your pits and sow them one by one into the next pits.
Where the last seed lands can earn an extra turn or a capture — a game of counting and foresight.

ch.say: There are more variants than you can count.
cards: Two rows of six; capture pits that reach two or three
Four rows of eight; said to be the most complex mancala
Asian relatives on boards of seven pits

ch.say: It was even played before kings.
stats: Known ways to play (by some counts)
cards: In West Africa it could be a special game played before kings and chiefs
Dig pits in the ground and use nuts or pebbles — that is how it spread everywhere

ch.say: Tap a card to flip it!
cards: No — it names the whole family of sowing games

ch.say: Read where the last seed will land!
p: Passed from hand to hand for over a thousand years — now the seeds are yours.
